The bassinet can look perfectly fine at bedtime, and that’s what makes this moment so uneasy. Your baby still settles there. Nothing looks dramatically wrong. But then you notice one new thing, a stronger push through the arms, a sideways scoot that wasn’t there last week, a body that suddenly seems to fill more of the sleep space—and the question changes fast: should the crib already be ready?

We think this is one of the most common first-time parent tensions because the bassinet stage rarely ends with a big announcement. More often, it ends in that almost-but-not-quite urgent window when age is less helpful than the actual safety timeline in front of you. Instead of waiting for a magic month, it helps to plan around limits, fit, and mobility so the move to a crib feels calm instead of rushed.

Bassinets are useful precisely because they’re small, simple, and easy to keep close in the early weeks. But those same qualities usually mean they have a shorter runway than many parents assume. The sleep space is smaller, the sides are lower than a full-size crib, and the product is designed for a very specific stage of early infancy.

That’s why the best question usually isn’t “What age do babies move from bassinet to crib?” It’s “Is this sleep space still the right one for my baby now?” In practice, three things matter most: the manufacturer’s limits for that specific bassinet, how your baby fits in the space, and whether new movement is starting to change the safety picture.

Safe sleep guidance in the U.S. is built around a firm, flat sleep surface and following product instructions closely. So if your bassinet manual gives weight limits, milestone cutoffs, or use restrictions, those directions come first. Age can give context, but it should not overrule the instructions for the actual product in your home.

How do you know it’s time to move from bassinet to crib?

If your baby is nearing any stated limit, the answer is usually not to squeeze a little more time out of the bassinet. It’s to get the crib ready now. The same is true if your baby suddenly looks cramped, is touching the sides more often, or is beginning the kinds of movements that make a smaller sleep space less forgiving.

We’d pay close attention to early mobility changes even before a dramatic milestone arrives. A first roll attempt, stronger pushing up, or the beginning of more forceful wiggling can be your sign that the bassinet’s useful window is closing. You do not need to wait until your baby looks unhappy there. You also do not need to wait for a night when the change feels obvious and urgent.

That distinction matters. Many babies still sleep well in a bassinet right up until the point when they are close to outgrowing it safely. Comfort and safety are related, but they are not the same thing. A baby can seem content and still be approaching the moment when a crib is the better overnight sleep space.

For anxious parents, “earlier” can sound like overreacting. We see it differently. If your baby is nearing a manufacturer limit or showing new movement, planning the crib transition before the bassinet becomes an obvious problem is often the calmer choice. It gives you time to assemble the crib carefully, check mattress fit, and get comfortable with the setup before you’re making decisions under pressure.

That’s also why we like treating the bassinet exit and the first crib setup changes as one connected timeline. If you move your baby into the crib this week, you may also be closer than you think to the first mattress-height adjustment. A sturdy, adjustable full-size crib makes that easier because it is designed to stay the long-term sleep base instead of becoming another short-lived stage to outgrow.

What should your crib setup be after the move?

Once you transition to the crib, start with the basics: a firm crib mattress that fits securely, a fitted sheet, and an otherwise bare sleep space. Then look at mattress height through the lens of what your baby is about to do next, not just what they did last week.

Many parents think of crib mattress height as a one-time assembly choice. In reality, it’s a sequence. The highest position can be useful early on, especially when you’re placing down a young infant often, but it is only appropriate while your baby’s mobility still makes that height safe according to the crib’s instructions. As your baby becomes more active, the mattress position that felt convenient at first may need to change sooner than expected.

This is where a well-made full-size crib earns its keep. When the crib is sturdy, easy to adjust, and built for everyday use beyond the newborn months, the transition feels less like a new furniture problem and more like a simple setup update. That long view is part of the appeal of a convertible crib: you’re not just solving tonight’s sleep question, but setting up a reliable base for the next stage too.

A simple milestone-to-setup map

  1. Rolling or clear roll attempts – If your baby is approaching this stage, the crib should already be ready. Review your crib manual and be prepared to move beyond the highest mattress setting if the instructions call for it.
  2. Pushing up on hands or gaining stronger upper-body control – Recheck mattress height before this strength turns into more lift and leverage than you expected.
  3. Sitting up – Lower the crib mattress according to the crib manufacturer’s guidance so the sleep space keeps an appropriate rail height as your baby becomes more upright.
  4. Pulling to stand – This is the milestone that makes delayed adjustments especially stressful. By this point, the mattress should already be at the appropriate lower setting for your crib, and parents should be watching closely for the next eventual transition later on.

The exact timing of each change depends on your baby and your crib’s instructions, which is why we always come back to manuals and milestones together. The important part is the mindset: don’t wait for each skill to fully arrive before thinking about the setup change it may require.

What this looks like in real life

Imagine a baby who still sleeps soundly in the bassinet at night and doesn’t seem bothered by it at all. On the surface, it feels easy to keep going. But the parents notice two things at once: the baby is taking up more of the sleep space, and tummy-time strength is turning into more forceful push-ups. Nothing has gone wrong. Still, the smarter move is clear—they check the bassinet limits, set up the crib now, and choose the right starting mattress height with the next milestone in mind.

That kind of proactive switch usually feels much better than a same-day scramble. It turns the transition into a planned handoff instead of a stressful reaction, and it gives the baby a stable sleep space that can keep working as development speeds up.

FAQ

Should I move my baby to a crib even if they still seem comfortable in the bassinet?

Yes, if they are nearing the bassinet’s limits or showing new mobility. Visible discomfort is not required for the crib to become the safer choice.

Does age alone tell me when to transition from bassinet to crib?

No. Age can be a rough reference point, but manufacturer limits, how your baby fits in the space, and changing movement matter more.

Should I start with the highest crib mattress setting?

Often, that setting is intended for the earliest stage, but the right answer depends on your crib’s instructions and your baby’s current mobility. If your baby is already close to rolling or pushing up strongly, it makes sense to think ahead before defaulting to the highest position.

What if my baby reaches a bassinet limit before I feel emotionally ready for the switch?

That feeling is very normal. We’d still treat the product limit as the decision point. The kindest thing you can do for yourself is make the crib ready before that day arrives, so the transition feels supported rather than abrupt.

What’s the most practical next step right now?

Check the bassinet manual, look honestly at your baby’s fit and movement, and set up the crib before the current arrangement feels questionable. A stable, adjustable crib that can handle the next mattress-height changes without fuss gives you a much calmer path through the months ahead.
